Messages.Body:
Recently, we've gotten into a debate over bleeding (mainly the non-card
kind). When our little group first started playing, we thought the Edge
was given to anyone for successfully bleeding. Later, someone noticed in
the non-bleed part of the rulebook that only a predator bleeding his prey
gets the Edge.

Well, last night, someone asked for me to find this reference to make sure
it was true. While I was reading the bleed section (action sub-section)
of the rulebook, it implied that you can only bleed your prey in this way.
At the end of this section, it states that a Methuselah making a
successful bleed gains the Edge. Now, the way we had been playing, this
was contradictory. So, I am now arguing that the only correct way to bleed
is to bleed your prey: the rulebook does not allow you to bleed anyone
else (by bleed, I mean the non-card variety). Later that night, I read up
on the thread concerning direct actions and bleeding, etc. They seemed
to back me up (only bleed your prey).

After looking through the rules and errata, etc, I have not found a
definite answer to my question:

Can you bleed anyone other than your prey?

If you cannot, I would be very happy. A certain member of our group likes
to bleed his predator to weaken him so he cannot bleed him back. He has
defeated me in many games doing this, because I have to defend against two
people...very difficult. Thanks in advance for any replies.

Way back when the game was being designed, the intent was to allow you to
bleed your prey only, as a (D) action. That's why the text on Cat Burglary
reads the way it does. The only way you could ever bleed someone else
was to use superior Cat Burglary (or get your bleed bounced by your Prey
playing Deflection or sup. Telepathic Misdirection).

Either way, successfully bleeding anybody gets you the edge, even though
you can only bleed your prey unless a card specifically says otherwise.

And life was good.

Then, WotC issued badly-thought-out errata that said the (D) symbol on a
card was not simply a reminder, but an override - allowing you to point
the action at any Methuselah. This action broke a few cards: Cat Burglary
and Rampage off the top of my head, while making other cards more powerful
(all of the (D) bleeders).

If this was the original intention, why weren't there any cards that
simply allowed a (D) bleed, without the bonus to bleed? Because that card
would've been worthless - it does nothing except note that the bleed is
(D), which is true of all bleeds, even the non-card ones.

And life was complicated and logic-free.

I'm not talking about making the game interesting. I'm talking about
rending the rules and grossly changing them (sledge hammer for computer
repair) in such a way that you break other pieces.

If the (D) merely describes the action, as it should IMO, then cards like
Cat Burglary and Rampage work as written.
This is how the original rules are written, and how the game came together, IMO.

Now, the errata pounded this (D) symbol thing until it looked like the (D)
is a modifier that allows you to direct the action anywhere.
Now Cat Burglary needs fixing.
Now Rampage is unblockable when used against yourself.
Now players (friends) in tournaments can gang up on somebody and guarantee a
loser much more easily.
Now Computer Hacking has a different flavor than a Laptop Computer, when they
both should obviously accomplish the same thing.

In article <3jfqfr$e...@redwood.cs.scarolina.edu>,

L. Scott Johnson <sjoh...@math.scarolina.edu> wrote:
>Now, the errata pounded this (D) symbol thing until it looked like the (D)
>is a modifier that allows you to direct the action anywhere.
>Now Cat Burglary needs fixing.

Cat Burglary needed fixing the moment it came out. It was
patently obvious that it was a screwed up card. The erratum in Duelist
#3 makes the wording on CB consistent with all of the other bleed cards
in the game.

>Now Rampage is unblockable when used against yourself.

Personally, I think that there's a note somewhere in WotC saying
that the wording should be changed on that card. When I was at GenCon
last year (where Jyhad was released for the first time), I saw several
of the WotC employees passing around a very long list of things that
needed to be fixed with Jyhad. It was a *lot* longer than all of the
errata I've seen. My guess is that Rampage is on there somewhere. It
should probably read "this is a non-directed action at +1 stealth...".

>Now players (friends) in tournaments can gang up on somebody and guarantee a
> loser much more easily.

That's a *very* subjective thing to say. We've been playing the
'official' (for lack of a better term) way the whole time, and so far we
have yet to see such a thing. But if we change the rules to play the
other way, I could just as easily say "This bites! Now when someone
makes an ass of themselves in the game, we can't do a thing to stop him
unless we've got vote cards! This makes these (D) bleed cards useless!"

>Now Computer Hacking has a different flavor than a Laptop Computer, when they
> both should obviously accomplish the same thing.

It's not obvious to me that they should both accomplish the same
thing. One is an action, and the other is Equipment. The action only
increases your bleed once, against anyone, and the equipment increses it
permanently against your prey (mainly, but it can also be used against
others with a card). Under *any* interpretation of the rules, the
Laptop is different by virtue of it being a permanent thing while the
hacking is temporary. Might as well say Tasha Morgan and J.S. Simmons
are also the same things as a Laptop and Comp. Hacking (which is also
inaccurate, as equipment is optional while retainers aren't).

I think that the design team has had one idea of what (D) means
the whole time, but has been doing a collossally bad job of explaining
it through the rules and rulings. A good treatise on (D) by the
designers would do this game wonders.

The official DTR: you can bleed only your prey without a card.
You can (D) bleed anyone with a card that says (D) bleed;
you get the Edge when you bleed successfully, whoever
you bleed. Cat Burglary needed an errata (and got one)
because of this ruling.

My personal oponion: you can bleed only your prey, with or
without a card. Only a few cards (Cat Burglary is one)
that specifically state on the card that you can
bleed somebody else are exceptions from this rule.
The original card text on Cat Burglary is correct;
the official errata is superfluous and misleading.
Those few cards that allow you to bleed somebody
other than your prey always restrict you to
bleed for 1 only; hence, their main function
is more for getting you the edge than for
really bleeding anybody you like for real harm.
Therefore, you do gain the edge whenever you
bleed successfully, whoever you bleed.

Let's compare the (according to the DTR) two main kinds
of cards that allow you to directly attack anybody:
(D) bleeds and Bum's Rush.

If you do a (D) bleed at +1, that player has to block you,
or he'll lose at least 2 pool. If players gang
up on somebody, he won't have enough (untapped)
minions to defend. There's no way he can defend against
this, except with a degenerate Telepathic Counter/
Telepathic Misdirection/WwEF deck.

If you Bum's Rush somebody, he does NOT have to tap to
block you. If his vampires have sufficient combat
ability, he can just meet the challenger. His
minions do not become tapped by your Bum's Rush,
unless you managed to parylyze him during the
combat. If several players gang up on somebody,
for sure he will have a lot of combats to fight,
but if he can come out of the combats without
taking too much damage, he can survive for
quite a while. He has a defense against the
gang-up Bum's Rush'ing strategy: he
can be good at combat.

If you (D) bleed him, he's tapped if he blocks,
and can't block subsequent bleeds (barring Wakes).
If you Bum's Rush him, he doesn't tap, can
still defend himself against subsequent Bum's
Rush'es, and even eventually blocking a bleed
from his predator.

Therefore, IMO, in the original design of the game,
(D) bleeds (on cards or otherwise) can only be
directed at your prey, while Bum's Rush can
be directed at anybody.

You know, you are the first person to ever bring this up to me.
I am usually the one who brings this up to others! Here's how I see it:
Grand Melee (GM) was a precursor to Jyhad. But the problem with GM was
twofold: there wasn't enough incentive to stick to your prey (1 VP,
woohoo!), and you had to limit range to keep the game managable. At
most, GM is for all interaction purposes a 5 player game.

What follows now is sheer supposition and opinion. I have no
way at the current time to know if it's true, but it's my best guess.

It started simply enough. Attack left from GM became bleed left
in Jyhad. Then he looked at the other parts of the game, including the
two problems from the GM.
To correct the first problem, he raised the incentive. But the
second problem was a lot trickier. To increase interaction, he dropped
the multiple turns going at once, and added political actions and
uniqueness. But they didn't add enough, so he added cards that could
affect any Methuselah to the game. Some of these were bleed cards (but
not all). Cool, the game worked fairly well this way.
Late in the playtesting process, while people were coming up
with symbols, and card layout had been partially done, it was decided
that those cards that could affect everyone would be called directed
actions, and would use the (D) symbol. As such, the concept wasn't
playtested as well as the rest (thus the big loophole about (D)'s
against yourself), and card layouts had to be changed quickly. The
result is that all bleed cards got the (D), and every card that affected
other players got the (D). Where possible the text was changed, but
some was missed (resulting in Cat Burglary and other cards that have
both the (D) and the text about "any Methuselah").
Thus we end up with what we have today. From this train of
thought, you can see why I believe that you *should* be able to bleed
across the table. Although I do think that perhaps not *every* bleed
card should be (D).

This seems like a good place to suggest an exmperiment: If you
don't play with (D) bleeds, try upping the blood prize for an ousting to
7 or 8 and allowing (D) bleeds. I'm curious to see if that will cure
the 'rampant bleeding' syndrome.

>bleeds?

the fact that I can make threats and back them up if necessary. There

need them as an interaction tool.

>Gangrel (or any rush) combat can still rush across the table. But you
>don't have to reach across the table to win anyway. Weenies do fine. So
>do straight Malks and Tremere, even without Eagle's sight.

interation purposes) with *any* deck I build. I don't want to have to

Eagle's Sight} if the subset of {titles|Bum's Rush|Eagle's Sight|Bleeds}

>deck even if I have no interest in votes. Even 1 vote makes a difference.

Not against a political deck. It just doesn't.

>How does Presence/Celerity work? I'm curious, as it sounds like my
>experimental (but not very functional) Toreador vote deck.

Bleeds up front, with the celerity for combat. You add a little
bite to it to your taste (Potence, Protean, or guns works well, but not
all 3), and throw in a few votes that match (never be without a Parity
Shift). The downside is that there's no subtlety to your actions (with
presence, it's call it first, vote or big bleed), but the upside is that
they'll probably be worse off than you after combat depending on your
bite. Celerity combat is second to none (although Brujah celerity
combat will still hurt...).

What you're doing right there is called a false dichotomy in
college logic classes. There are more than two kinds of actions.

There are three categories of actions:
1. Undirected actions
2. Bleeds, which are directed and restricted to prey, and
3. Actions which have the (D) symbol, and can be directed at anyone.

The directed bleed cards (with the (D) move actions which are normally
category 2 into category 3. (From 'directed at prey' to 'directed
at anyone'.)

As long as you all argue from the premise that there are only two
kinds of actions, you're going to go around and around and around.
I think most of the readers of this thread are ready to get off
this merry-go-round.

translation of attack left Magic). Bleed is a fundamental part of the
game that cannot be altered without changing the basic chemistry of the
game. From discussion here, it is obvious to me that (D)'s are not as
fundamental as bleeds, and I have put forth the supposition that they
were in fact changed to symbols instead of explicit text on cards late
in the design process.
Therefore, it seems to me that there are two sections of the
rules which conflict on this issue, the definition of bleed and the fact
that 'if (D) doesn't appear it isn't directed' is stated. Since bleed
is more fundamental to the game and was probably written early on, I
tend to put more stock in that section of the rules than in what I
suppose was a relatively hastily written section of the rules, so I put
my credence in the bleed statement.
Therefore I believe that "bleed" on a card means that you take a
normal, directed bleed against your prey.

As a sidebar, I will also state that I believe that *someone* in
the layout process believed differently, and thus stuck a (D) symbol on
all cards that had bleed, not understanding the differences between
normal actions and bleed actions. But this is based far less on
established arguements than the above conclusion.

>I speculate they'd be embarrassed that their (D) bleed ruling makes it
>impossible for a bleed action card to function as a normal bleed without
>special wording.

I think, rather, that they did not predict that people would
read the removal of the (D) symbol as the removal of the directedness
(directed nature?) of a bleed, since the concept was so foreign to their
conception of how the game worked.

>As I've said before, their blindness to side effect of their changes makes
>me very concerned about their suitability to arbitrate rules disputes.

Nobody has a problem with better than 90% of their rulings. It's
the ones that are subtle that shake people.
However, please note that there *are* those of us who agree with
the (D) bleed ruling, meaning that no matter how strongly you believe
one way, you must acknowledge that their ruling is a valid possible
interpretation.

ordinary non-directed actions that can only be blocked

Timing of ousts is often critical. If the predator can't mount some
serious bleeds, he may take 2 or even 3 turns to oust a 6, even with no
blockers. In any case, he will get jumped by his own predator first, and
a good reason to oust someone is to give 6 pool to his doomed predator
just to keep him in the game a bit longer. Surviving a turn or two also
allows retaliation, also a big disadvantage.

IME, CTBs often go at rush decks that have basically exterminated all
their predator's vampires. In those circumstances the predator can't
oust, only the grandpredator. It's an ideal situation to give blood to
the predator, because he's unlikely to be able to do much with it.

My opinion is that if the game is `perfectly' balanced out,
it will be possible to tune any deck against any other `static'
deck WITHOUT using clan hosers. If the only way to stop a
deck from being `unbeatable' is using clan hosers, then
in my opinion the game has a balance problem.

Stone-paper-scissors is a perfectly balanced game. Every
gesture has a `hoser' to counter it; anybody who constantly
makes the same gesture will lose. Yet this does not make
S-P-S too much of `a great game' other than as a method
to randomly determine something.

Mathematically, clan hosers work like S-P-S. Suppose that there
are three `unbeatable' deck configurations, each using a different
clan, that cannot be beaten by any decks other than these 3
without using clan hosers. Then the game would reduce to merely
trying to guess which of the 3 `unbeatable' decks your opponent
is using, and putting in lots of the appropriate clan hoser.
IMO, clan hosers reduce (to a certain extent) the `level' of
the game to that of S-P-S. Clan hosers is IMO a cheap substitute
of designing and tuning a deck strategy to counter a deck.
IMO relying on clan hosers to `balance' a game is a cheap game design
element substitute of carefully balancing out the core elements
of the game system.

That is obvious - the `Color Hosers' from Magic, such as Karma,
Tsunami, etc. Also lesser ones, such as the Exorcist. Cards

based on their functions within the game system (such as
"Terror" countering "Regeneration").

interaction. A Dodge cancels a strike, and that is similar.

part of the game system.

Joseph Cochran (js...@discus.ise.vt.edu) wrote:

Well, in Magic they were called Colour Hosers - they were cards that only
worked against a specific colour rather than all cards of that type in
play. Examples of the top of my head: (freely mixing and abusing
terminology...)

Flashfires - Red card to burn all White land in play
Tsunami - Green card to burn all Blue land in play
Red Elemental Blast - counter any Blue card as it is being played
Blue elemental Blast - as above, but for Blue vs. Red.
Gloom - Black card that made all White cards more expensive to cast
Deathgrip/Lifegrip - Black/Green card that stayed in play and could (for a
cost) counter any Green/Black spell as it was cast.
Karma - White card that hurt you every turn for every Black land you had.

There are more, and this list is just from the basic set. The main
difference between Magic and Jyhad (in this respect) is that colours had
certain pre-defined 'enemies', and had cards to counter the spells of
those enemy colours. In Jyhad, there are no pre-set enmities (a good
thing, IMHO, as it increases flexibility) and anyone can use a 'clan
hoser' as they are all Master Cards instead of discipline-specific cards.

Please do _not_ add to this list - it is an example only and I have no
intention of turning this into a MtG thread.

>

>For example, Press to end cancels a Press to continue, but this
>is more of a game function thing rather than as a card identity
>interaction. A Dodge cancels a strike, and that is similar.
>Clan Hosers attack cards of a certain identity, in a manner
>with little regard to their function within the more coherent
>part of the game system.
>
>I'm surprised that anyone can't see the obvious connection.

Force and counterforce is an idea that has been around forever.
The idea that there is something that is inherently opposite to
something else by virtue of its identity is a concept that is at the
basis of humanity, from God and the devil to life and death. Magic was
set up with these adversarial relationships already in place, so it is
perfectly natural that each color should have specific things in it to
hurt those colors that are its enemies for no other reason than their
identity.
Jyhad, on the other hand, has no inherent opposites (although
one of the variants made an attempt to do that), and thus, there are no
cards that oppose one another due to strict identity. However, each
clan has a weakness, represented by their hoser card. There is no
opposition, no connection between one clan and the other, and no tie to
basic force-counterforce tendencies. Hosers are much more related to
the weaknesses of the clans from the RPG than to red vs blue in Magic
(although I do not doubt that the whole 'clan hoser' set was conceived
as one thing).
So, you see, I don't think that there *is* an obvious
connection, merely a superficial one that disappears when you look at
the games more closely.

Messages.Author: Owen Reynolds
Messages.Body:
The discussiuon on clan-hosers is missing a "practical" aspect which
I thought I'd try to add.

It seems to me that clan-hosers are there for 2 reasons. The first
is from Magic: a single clan/color has certain obvious advantages
(tighter disciplines, access to "helps all clan X" cards, and so on.)
The "hosers" are there to encourage you to consider a little more
diversity.
Secondly, which I agree is a silly reason, the crypt is the focus
of a good deck, so if some strategy turns out to be "optimal" than
people will tend to include a higher percentage of hosers for the
vampires used, making it less optimal.

For purpose number 2, ANY hoser would work. Suppose someone has a
unstoppable crypt made of Rabbits and Pigs. As long as the other players
can play cards which do anything at all to Rabbit and Pigs (tap 1, make
them lose a blood, anything) the hosers "work" to slow him down.

For purpose number 1, the hosers SUCK. The biggest problem are the
single-vamp hosers (Malks, Brujah, Gangrels, Nosfer, Toreador.) They
do nothing to encourage you to include a few non-clan vampires in a
mostly-1-clan crypt. In fact, they do the opposite.
Suppose you have 11 vampires picked out and just need a 12th that
fits in well (and don't want to use a duplicate.) Adding one from one
of the aforementioned clans gives someone a chance to use a clan-hoser
on you to full effect (for example, adding Uma Hatch to a weenie voter
deck without other Brujah is asking for her to Frenzy while calling a
vote.) Lots of people toss a Malk Dementia in their decks since Malks
are so hated. I'd be a fool to include Normal in my "Nosfers with
Concealed Weapons" deck.

Other hoser comments:

Cultivated Blood Shortage: This is easily the most deadly hoser. An all-
Ventrue deck can be hit for 4 net blood loss in 1 turn by this.
It's removed at +1 stealth, right? (I traded mine away.) This still
makes me never want to play an all-Ventrue deck twice in a row with
the same people.

Nosferatu Putresense: This isn't even a real clan-hoser -- it's a strategy
hoser. I've got a potence/fortitude combat deck that uses Nosfers (and
a silly 4-card limit) that this card could destroy. Someone else's
Nosfer/Ventrue vote deck would hardly notice this card being played.

Gangrel De-evolution: This has also been noted as not a real clan-hoser,
as well. I've got a Gangrel "all minions go to torpor" deck. Someone
De-evolves half my vampires. My strategy is still unchanged, it will
just take me longer to oust my helpless prey, or I just use Gypsies and
Army of Rats.

>more elegantly within the game system by their lack of certain disciplines.

More variety, more strategies to try out. Good thing, IMO.

>> So, you see, I don't think that there *is* an obvious
>>connection, merely a superficial one that disappears when you look at
>>the games more closely.
>
>On the contrary, although looking at the superficial aspects of
>the game, such as the setting, theme, ect. Clan Hosers
>are significantly different from color hosers, in terms of
>game mechanics, their functions are very similar.

No, I don't believe that they are. They do have their
similarities, but in Magic, you are forced to use a particular color to
hose another color (back to the identity thing). This limits your
strategies if you want to use those hosers. Clan hosers require no
specific strategy to implement (no conflict by identity), and thus
broaden the strategies you can use. From a game mechanics point of
view, that's the total opposite of color hosers.
